title: Reviewing the Whole Sequence
bigQuestion: How do you choose the right verb form and the right connecting word when a whole essay, not a single sentence, is on the line?

story.title: Two Red Pens
story.kicker: Two seniors trade essays on a Tuesday afternoon and discover that finding someone else's mistakes is the fastest way to learn your own.
paragraphs: Marisol and Andrés sit at a corner table in the library of their high school in Cicero, just west of Chicago. Their Spanish teacher has paired them up to edit each other's essays before the final draft is due. Marisol's topic is her grandmother's bakery in Little Village. Andrés wrote about the soccer league at his park. Each of them holds a red pen and a printed page, and neither one wants to go first.

Andrés starts reading Marisol's second paragraph aloud. "Cuando yo era niña, mi abuela abrió la panadería." (When I was a girl, my grandmother opened the bakery.) He stops. "Era for the background, abrió for the event. That is right." Then he reads the next line: "Ella trabajaba allí por veinte años." He circles trabajaba. "Twenty years, finished, counted. That should be trabajó." Marisol groans, then nods. She has heard both forms her whole life; she has just never had to choose one on paper.

Marisol takes her turn with his essay. "Es importante que los niños tienen un lugar seguro." (It is important that the kids have a safe place.) She underlines tienen. "Es importante que is a trigger. It wants tengan." Andrés looks at the sentence for a long moment. "I know that rule," he says. "I just did not see it while I was writing." She finds two more: a sentence that begins with *sin embargo* (however) but adds a point instead of contrasting one, and *por lo tanto* (therefore) glued to a sentence it does not follow from.

By the end of the hour, each essay has a dozen circles and every circle has a reason next to it. Their teacher stops by and reads over their shoulders. "You know more grammar than you think," she tells them. "The problem is never one sentence. The problem is keeping the whole map in your head at once." This chapter is that map: the tenses, the moods, the connectors, and a routine for catching your own errors before a classmate has to.
story.think: Why is it often easier to spot a wrong verb form in someone else's writing than in your own? What would you need to do to read your own essay the way Andrés read Marisol's?

lessons.title: Present and Present Perfect
lessons.mainIdea: The present tense states what is happening or what is usually true, while the present perfect (he hablado) reports what has happened up to now.
reading: Marisol's first paragraph opens with two sentences that look alike but do different work. "Mi abuela trabaja en la panadería todos los días" (My grandmother works in the bakery every day). "Mi abuela ha trabajado allí toda su vida" (My grandmother has worked there her whole life). The first is the simple *present*: a habit, a fact that is true right now. The second is the *present perfect*, built from the helper verb *haber* plus a past participle, and it reaches from the past up to this moment.

The helper is easy to memorize because it is short: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han. The *participle* is the verb's -ado or -ido form: trabajar → trabajado, comer → comido, vivir → vivido. Put them together and you have he trabajado, has comido, hemos vivido. The participle never changes for the subject; only the helper does. English speakers sometimes write "he trabajo" because English drops the ending in "I have worked" only in speech, not in the verb. In Spanish the -ado is not optional.

A handful of participles are irregular, and they show up constantly in essays: hecho (done, made), dicho (said), escrito (written), visto (seen), puesto (put), vuelto (returned), abierto (opened), roto (broken), muerto (died). "He escrito tres borradores" (I have written three drafts). "¿Has visto la película?" (Have you seen the movie?) Writing "he escribido" is the single most common participle error, because the regular pattern is so strong.

When do you choose the perfect over the simple present or the preterite? Use it for experience up to now ("Nunca he estado en Guatemala," I have never been to Guatemala) and for recent events still connected to the present ("Hoy he terminado el ensayo," Today I have finished the essay). Speakers in much of Latin America prefer the preterite for that second use, "Hoy terminé el ensayo," and both are correct. The rule that never changes: nothing goes between the helper and the participle. "No lo he visto," never "he no visto" or "he lo visto."

words.d: the present perfect — haber plus a participle: he hablado (I have spoken); reports what has happened up to now
the helper verb of the perfect tenses: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han; never used alone to mean to have (that is tener)
the participle — the -ado or -ido form of a verb (hablado, comido); irregulars include hecho, dicho, escrito, visto
written — irregular participle of escribir: He escrito una carta (I have written a letter); never escribido

look.title: One Day at the Bakery
look.text: Marisol describes her grandmother's day in two layers. Present: Mi abuela abre la panadería a las cinco. Hace pan dulce y conchas. Los vecinos compran café antes del trabajo. Present perfect: Este año ha abierto una segunda vitrina. Ha hecho más de mil conchas este mes. Los vecinos han vuelto todos los días.
look.prompt: Find each helper verb and its participle. Which three participles are irregular, and what would the wrong regular form have looked like?

check.q: Yo ___ (escribir) tres borradores del ensayo.
check.why: The present perfect for yo is he plus the participle, and escribir has the irregular participle escrito.

check.q: What does "Nunca hemos estado en Puerto Rico" mean?
choices: We are never in Puerto Rico.
We have never been to Puerto Rico.
We never went to Puerto Rico last year.
We will never be in Puerto Rico.
check.why: Hemos estado is the present perfect of estar, reporting experience up to now: we have never been.

check.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
check.why: Nothing goes between haber and the participle; no and the pronoun lo both go before he.

lessons.title: Preterite Beside Imperfect
lessons.mainIdea: The preterite reports a completed event, the imperfect paints background and habit, and a longer passage needs both working together.
reading: Andrés circled trabajaba in Marisol's essay, and he was right. "Ella trabajó allí veinte años" (She worked there for twenty years) counts a finished stretch of time, and a counted, finished stretch takes the *preterite*. The *imperfect* trabajaba would say she used to work there, with no edges on the time. Both tenses talk about the past; the difference is whether the writer is looking at an event with a beginning and an end, or at a scene that was going on.

The quickest way to keep them apart in an essay is to sort every past verb into two jobs. Job one, the imperfect: what things were like, what people used to do, age, time, weather, and what was happening when something else happened. "Era invierno. Hacía frío. Yo tenía ocho años. Mi abuela amasaba el pan." (It was winter. It was cold. I was eight. My grandmother was kneading the bread.) Job two, the preterite: what happened next, one event after another. "Entró un cliente. Pidió veinte conchas. Mi abuela sonrió." (A customer came in. He ordered twenty conchas. My grandmother smiled.)

The two jobs meet in one sentence all the time, and that sentence is the one students get wrong most. "Mi abuela amasaba el pan cuando entró el cliente" (My grandmother was kneading the bread when the customer came in). The imperfect sets the scene; the preterite interrupts it. Reverse them and the sentence stops making sense. Writing "amasó… cuando entraba" would say she finished kneading at some point during his slow entrance, which is not what happened.

A few verbs shift meaning between the two tenses, and an editor should know them. *Sabía* means I knew; *supe* means I found out. *Conocía* means I knew a person; *conocí* means I met them. *Quería* means I wanted; *quise* means I tried, and *no quise* means I refused. "Conocí a mi mejor amigo en la panadería" (I met my best friend at the bakery) is a single event, so it takes the preterite. Choosing conocía there would tell the reader you already knew him, which contradicts the story.

words.d: the preterite — a completed past event or a counted stretch of time: Trabajó veinte años (She worked twenty years)
the imperfect — background, habit, age, time and weather in the past: Tenía ocho años (I was eight)
I found out — the preterite of saber changes meaning; the imperfect sabía means I knew
I met — the preterite of conocer marks the first meeting; conocía means I already knew someone

look.title: The Morning the Oven Broke
look.text: Read Marisol's paragraph and sort the verbs. Era un sábado de diciembre. La panadería estaba llena y todos querían pan dulce. De repente el horno dejó de funcionar. Mi abuela no dijo nada. Llamó a mi tío, que sabía arreglar cualquier cosa. Mientras esperábamos, ella vendía el pan que ya tenía. Mi tío llegó en veinte minutos y a las nueve el horno funcionaba otra vez.
look.prompt: List every preterite and every imperfect. For sabía, funcionaba and dijo, explain in one phrase why that tense fits.

check.q: Mi abuela ___ (amasar) el pan cuando entró el cliente.
check.why: The action in progress when another event interrupts takes the imperfect: amasaba.

check.q: Which sentence means "I met my best friend at the bakery"?
choices: Conocí a mi mejor amigo en la panadería.
Conocía a mi mejor amigo en la panadería.
Conozco a mi mejor amigo en la panadería.
He conocido mi mejor amigo en la panadería.
check.why: Meeting someone for the first time is a single event, so conocer takes the preterite conocí, with the personal a.

check.q: Why is "Ella trabajó allí veinte años" preterite rather than imperfect?
choices: Because the twenty years are a finished, counted stretch of time.
Because ella is a third-person subject.
Because the sentence describes a habit.
check.why: A completed period with a stated length is viewed as one whole event, which is the job of the preterite.

lessons.title: Future and Conditional
lessons.mainIdea: The future (hablaré) and the conditional (hablaría) share one stem and one set of irregulars; the future says what will happen, the conditional what would happen.
reading: Marisol ends her essay by looking ahead. "El próximo año mi prima abrirá una segunda panadería" (Next year my cousin will open a second bakery). Then she softens it: "Yo trabajaría con ella si tuviera tiempo" (I would work with her if I had time). Abrirá is the *future*; trabajaría is the *conditional*. Both are built the same way: keep the whole infinitive, then add the ending. Future endings are é, ás, á, emos, éis, án. Conditional endings are ía, ías, ía, íamos, íais, ían.

Because the endings attach to the full infinitive, every -ar, -er and -ir verb behaves alike: abriré, abrirás, abrirá; comería, comerías, comería. That makes these two tenses the most regular in the language. The accent marks are not decoration. Hablara without an accent is a subjunctive form; hablará with one is the future. Hablaria is not a word; hablaría is. When an editor sees a future or conditional without its accent, the form is wrong.

Twelve common verbs shorten their stem, and the shortened stem serves both tenses: tener → tendr- (tendré, tendría), poner → pondr-, salir → saldr-, venir → vendr-, poder → podr-, saber → sabr-, querer → querr-, haber → habr-, hacer → har-, decir → dir-, caber → cabr-, valer → valdr-. "Habrá más clientes" (There will be more customers). "Diría la verdad" (I would tell the truth). Students who learn the irregulars for the future get the conditional for free.

Spanish also uses these tenses to guess. "¿Qué hora es? Serán las cinco" (What time is it? It must be about five). "¿Dónde estaba tu tío? Estaría en el taller" (Where was your uncle? He was probably in the shop). The future guesses about now; the conditional guesses about the past. In everyday speech, ir a plus an infinitive often replaces the future for plans: "Voy a abrir la panadería a las cinco." Both are correct. In a formal essay, the one-word future sounds more polished.

words.d: the future tense — infinitive plus é, ás, á, emos, éis, án: abriré (I will open)
the conditional — infinitive plus ía, ías, ía, íamos, íais, ían: trabajaría (I would work)
I will have — tener uses the shortened stem tendr- in both the future (tendré) and the conditional (tendría)
there will be — the future of hay; the conditional is habría (there would be)

look.title: Two Versions of Next Year
look.text: Andrés writes his plans twice. Confident: El año que viene la liga tendrá más equipos. Haremos un torneo en junio. Los padres vendrán a ver los partidos. Cautious: Con más dinero, la liga tendría más equipos. Haríamos un torneo en junio. Los padres vendrían a ver los partidos.
look.prompt: Underline the stem each verb pair shares, and say what changed between the two versions and what did not.

check.q: Which form means "I would tell"?
check.why: Decir uses the shortened stem dir-; the conditional ending -ía gives diría, I would tell.

check.q: Mañana ___ (haber) más clientes en la panadería.
check.why: Haber shortens to habr- and takes the future ending -á: habrá, there will be.

check.q: What is wrong with the form "hablara" in the sentence "Mañana ella hablara con el jefe"?
choices: It needs the accent: hablará is the future; hablara is a subjunctive form.
It should be hablaría because mañana is in the future.
The subject should come after the verb.
Nothing; hablara is the correct future.
check.why: The future has a written accent on the ending; without it, hablara is the imperfect subjunctive, a different form.

lessons.title: Triggers and the Present Subjunctive
lessons.mainIdea: A trigger phrase plus que plus a change of subject sends the second verb into the present subjunctive, built from the yo form with the opposite vowel.
reading: Marisol underlined tienen in "Es importante que los niños tienen un lugar seguro." The sentence has all three parts of the *subjunctive* pattern. A trigger: es importante. The word *que*. A new subject: los niños. When those three line up, the verb after que changes its shape: "Es importante que los niños tengan un lugar seguro." The subjunctive is a mood, not a tense; it does not say when something happens, it says the speaker is wishing, judging, doubting or feeling rather than reporting.

Building it is a two-step routine. Step one: take the yo form of the present and drop the -o. Tener → tengo → teng-. Hablar → hablo → habl-. Conocer → conozco → conozc-. Step two: add the opposite vowel endings. For -ar verbs use e: hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen. For -er and -ir verbs use a: tenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengáis, tengan. Starting from the yo form is what keeps the irregular stem: tenga, conozca, salga, diga.

Six verbs do not follow the routine, and every essay uses at least two of them: ser → sea, estar → esté, ir → vaya, haber → haya, saber → sepa, dar → dé. "Espero que sea fácil" (I hope it is easy). "No creo que haya tiempo" (I do not think there is time). Writing "es" or "hay" after those triggers is the mistake to hunt for.

The triggers fall into families you can list on a card. Wishes and wants: querer que, esperar que, ojalá que. Emotions: me alegra que, temo que, es triste que. Impersonal judgments: es importante que, es necesario que, es mejor que. Recommendations: recomendar que, sugerir que, pedir que. Doubt and denial: dudar que, no creer que, no es verdad que. One check catches most errors: if the subject does not change, there is no que and no subjunctive. "Quiero tener un lugar seguro" (I want to have a safe place) keeps the plain infinitive.

words.d: the subjunctive — the mood for wishes, judgments, doubt and emotion: Es importante que tengan (It is important that they have)
it is important that — an impersonal judgment; subjunctive follows when a new subject appears
they have (subjunctive) — from the yo form tengo, drop -o, add -an; the indicative is tienen
there is (subjunctive) — the irregular subjunctive of hay: No creo que haya tiempo
I hope that, if only — an Arabic-rooted word that always takes the subjunctive: Ojalá que llueva

look.title: The Coach's Wish List
look.text: Andrés quotes his coach. Quiero que los niños lleguen a tiempo. Es necesario que cada equipo tenga un adulto. Espero que la ciudad arregle el campo. No creo que haya dinero para luces nuevas. Ojalá que los padres vengan a los partidos. Me alegra que ustedes estén aquí.
look.prompt: For each sentence name the trigger family (wish, judgment, emotion, doubt) and write the indicative form the verb was built from.

check.q: Es importante que los niños ___ (tener) un lugar seguro.
check.why: Es importante que is an impersonal trigger with a new subject, so tener takes the present subjunctive tengan, built from tengo.

check.q: Which sentence correctly uses an irregular subjunctive?
choices: Espero que el examen es fácil.
Espero que el examen está fácil.
Espero que el examen sea fácil.
Espero que el examen ser fácil.
check.why: Ser has the irregular subjunctive sea; es and está are indicative, and the bare infinitive cannot follow que with a new subject.

check.q: Why does "Quiero tener un lugar seguro" use the infinitive instead of the subjunctive?
choices: Because querer never triggers the subjunctive.
Because the sentence is in the past.
Because the subject does not change, so there is no que clause.
check.why: The subjunctive needs a change of subject after que; with one subject, Spanish uses the infinitive.

lessons.title: Past Subjunctive and If
lessons.mainIdea: The imperfect subjunctive comes from the ellos preterite with -ra endings, follows past triggers, and pairs with the conditional in imagined if-sentences.
reading: Marisol's last paragraph has the sentence "Yo trabajaría con ella si tuviera tiempo." Andrés checks the second half. Tuviera is the *imperfect subjunctive*, and it is built from a form students already know: the ellos form of the preterite. Tener → tuvieron → drop -ron → tuvie- → add -ra. Hablar → hablaron → hablara. Ir and ser → fueron → fuera. Decir → dijeron → dijera. Because the base is the preterite, every preterite irregular comes along automatically.

The endings are -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran, with one accent in the nosotros form: habláramos, tuviéramos. That accent falls on the vowel before -ramos. Missing it is a small error, but it is the kind an editor is paid to catch. Spain and formal writing also use a second set of endings in -se (hablase, tuviese); they mean the same thing, and the -ra set is what most Chicago classrooms teach.

The imperfect subjunctive has two main jobs. Job one: the same triggers as before, but in the past. "Mi abuela quería que yo aprendiera a hacer pan" (My grandmother wanted me to learn to make bread). "Era importante que los niños tuvieran un lugar seguro." When the trigger verb is in the preterite or imperfect, the verb after que shifts to the past subjunctive to match.

Job two is the if-sentence about an imagined world. The pattern is fixed: si plus the imperfect subjunctive, comma, the conditional. "Si tuviera tiempo, trabajaría con ella." "Si la liga tuviera más dinero, compraría luces" (If the league had more money, it would buy lights). Two mistakes to hunt for: the conditional inside the si clause ("si tendría" is never correct) and the present indicative where an imagined world is meant. "Si tengo tiempo, trabajo con ella" is a fine sentence, but it says the time is a real possibility, not a wish.

words.d: the imperfect subjunctive — from the ellos preterite: tuvieron → tuviera; follows past triggers and si
had (past subjunctive) — Si tuviera tiempo, iría (If I had time, I would go); never si tendría
were, went (past subjunctive) — serves both ser and ir: Si yo fuera rica (If I were rich)
wanted (someone) to — a past trigger that takes the imperfect subjunctive: Quería que yo aprendiera

look.title: Building Four Past Subjunctives
look.text: Walk the routine on four verbs. poder: pudieron → pudie- → pudiera. hacer: hicieron → hicie- → hiciera. estar: estuvieron → estuvie- → estuviera. venir: vinieron → vinie- → viniera. Now use each one: Si pudiera, iría. Si hiciera calor, jugaríamos afuera. Si estuviera aquí mi abuelo, estaría orgulloso. Quería que vinieran todos.
look.prompt: Try the routine on decir, ser and saber. Which one gives the same form for two different verbs, and how does context tell them apart?

check.q: Si la liga ___ (tener) más dinero, compraría luces.
check.why: An imagined if-sentence uses the imperfect subjunctive after si: tuviera. The conditional belongs in the other half.

check.q: Mi abuela quería que yo ___ (aprender) a hacer pan.
check.why: Quería que is a past trigger, so the verb after que takes the imperfect subjunctive aprendiera, from aprendieron.

check.q: What does "Si yo fuera rica, abriría otra panadería" mean?
choices: When I am rich, I open another bakery.
If I was rich, I opened another bakery.
If I were rich, I would open another bakery.
Because I am rich, I will open another bakery.
check.why: Fuera plus the conditional abriría describes an imagined situation: if I were rich, I would open.

lessons.title: Choosing the Form from Context
lessons.mainIdea: Before picking a verb form, ask three questions in order: when, is it finished or background, and is it a fact or a wish, doubt or judgment.
reading: Andrés and Marisol were not short on rules; they were short on a way to apply them fast. Their teacher gave them three questions to ask about any verb in an essay. First, when: past, present or future? Second, if past, is it a completed event or a scene in the background? Third, is the verb reporting a fact, or does a trigger before que turn it into a wish, judgment, doubt or emotion? Answering in that order narrows a dozen forms down to one.

Try it on a line from Andrés's essay: "Cuando yo (ser) niño, mi padre siempre me (llevar) al parque, y allí (conocer) a mi mejor amigo." Ser: past, background, fact → era. Llevar: past, habit marked by siempre, fact → llevaba. Conocer: past, one completed event, fact → conocí. "Cuando yo era niño, mi padre siempre me llevaba al parque, y allí conocí a mi mejor amigo." Three past verbs, two tenses, no guessing.

Now a line with triggers: "Mi padre quería que yo (jugar) todos los sábados, y hoy espero que mi hijo (hacer) lo mismo." Jugar: past trigger quería que, new subject → jugara. Hacer: present trigger espero que, new subject → haga. Notice that the same question, is there a trigger, sends one verb to the past subjunctive and one to the present subjunctive, and the difference is only the tense of the trigger.

Context also settles cases where the form alone is ambiguous. "Cuando llegue mi tío, arreglará el horno" (When my uncle arrives, he will fix the oven): llegue is subjunctive because the arrival is still ahead. "Cuando llega mi tío, siempre arregla algo" (When my uncle arrives, he always fixes something): llega is indicative because it is a habit. The word cuando did not decide; the timeline did. Readers of a whole essay feel these choices even when they cannot name them, which is why a single wrong tense can make a paragraph feel confusing.

words.d: the context — the words and timeline around a verb that decide its form; the same cuando can take llega or llegue
when he or she arrives (future, not yet happened) — cuando takes the subjunctive for a pending event
always — a habit marker that usually points to the imperfect in the past: siempre me llevaba
the draft — the version of an essay you edit; primer borrador is the first draft

look.title: Twelve Blanks, Three Questions
look.text: Apply the three questions to Marisol's paragraph. Mi abuela (llegar) a Chicago en 1985. No (tener) dinero, pero (saber) hacer pan. Al principio (vender) conchas desde su cocina. Un vecino le (decir) que (abrir) una tienda. Ella (dudar) que (ser) posible. Hoy la panadería (tener) tres empleados, y mi abuela quiere que yo la (ayudar) los sábados. Si yo (poder), (trabajar) allí todos los días.
look.prompt: Fill each blank and write the question that decided it: when, finished or background, or trigger. Compare answers with a partner and argue any disagreement.

check.q: Cuando yo ___ (ser) niño, mi padre siempre me llevaba al parque.
check.why: Age in the past is background, and the sentence describes a habit with siempre, so ser takes the imperfect era.

check.q: Cuando ___ (llegar) mi tío, arreglará el horno.
check.why: The arrival has not happened yet and the main verb is future, so cuando takes the present subjunctive llegue.

check.q: Mi padre quería que yo ___ (jugar) todos los sábados.
check.why: The trigger quería que is in the past, so the second verb takes the imperfect subjunctive jugara.

lessons.title: Contrast Connectors
lessons.mainIdea: Sin embargo, en cambio and aunque all signal contrast, but each one joins ideas in a different shape and aunque can change the mood of the verb after it.
reading: Marisol found a *sin embargo* (however) in Andrés's essay that was doing the wrong job. "La liga tiene cien niños. Sin embargo, tiene veinte entrenadores." (The league has a hundred kids. However, it has twenty coaches.) Nothing in the second sentence contradicts the first; the connector promised a turn that never came. A *connector* is a word or phrase that tells the reader how the next idea relates to the last one. Use the wrong one and the reader stumbles even when every verb is right.

Three contrast connectors carry most essays. *Sin embargo* opens a new sentence and reverses expectation: "La liga tiene cien niños. Sin embargo, no tiene un campo con luces." (The league has a hundred kids. However, it has no field with lights.) It is always followed by a comma. *En cambio* (on the other hand, instead) sets two things side by side: "Mi barrio no tiene canchas; en cambio, Pilsen tiene tres." (My neighborhood has no courts; Pilsen, on the other hand, has three.) *Pero* (but) works inside one sentence and is the everyday choice; sin embargo is its formal cousin.

*Aunque* (although, even though) is the one connector that can change a verb. With the indicative it concedes a fact: "Aunque llueve, jugamos" (Even though it is raining, we play). With the subjunctive it concedes a possibility: "Aunque llueva, jugaremos" (Even if it rains, we will play). English separates the two with even though and even if; Spanish keeps one word and moves the difference into the verb, which is a pattern you have seen all through this course.

An editor's test for any contrast connector: cover it, read the two ideas, and ask whether the second pushes against the first. If it does not, replace the connector with *además* (besides, moreover) or simply start the sentence plainly. Andrés fixed his line to "La liga tiene cien niños; sin embargo, solo tiene veinte entrenadores" by adding solo, which turns twenty coaches into a shortage and earns the however.

words.d: the connector — a word or phrase such as sin embargo or además that shows how one idea relates to the last
however, nevertheless — reverses expectation at the start of a sentence, always followed by a comma
on the other hand, instead — sets two cases side by side: Yo prefiero el pan; en cambio, ella prefiere el café
although, even though, even if — takes the indicative for a known fact and the subjunctive for a possibility

look.title: Same Facts, Four Connectors
look.text: Facts: the bakery is small; it sells out every day. Read the four joins. La panadería es pequeña, pero se agota todos los días. La panadería es pequeña. Sin embargo, se agota todos los días. La panadería de mi abuela es pequeña; en cambio, la del centro es enorme. Aunque la panadería sea pequeña, seguirá vendiendo todo.
look.prompt: Which sentence changed the second fact to make the connector work? Which one uses the subjunctive, and what does that verb add to the meaning?

check.q: Which sentence uses sin embargo correctly?
choices: Tengo hambre. Sin embargo, quiero comer.
La liga es popular. Sin embargo, tiene muchos jugadores.
Estudié mucho. Sin embargo, no aprobé el examen.
Hace sol. Sin embargo, hace buen tiempo.
check.why: Sin embargo must introduce a turn against expectation; studying hard and still failing is the only real contrast.

check.q: What does "Aunque llueva, jugaremos" mean?
choices: Even though it is raining, we play.
Because it rains, we will play.
Even if it rains, we will play.
check.why: The subjunctive llueva after aunque presents rain as a possibility, not a fact: even if it rains.

check.q: Mi barrio no tiene canchas; ___, Pilsen tiene tres.
check.why: En cambio sets two cases side by side; además would add, por lo tanto would conclude, and aunque needs a clause.

lessons.title: Adding and Concluding
lessons.mainIdea: Además adds a point, por lo tanto draws a conclusion, and a connector should only appear where the logic between two ideas truly exists.
reading: The second connector Marisol circled was *por lo tanto* (therefore) glued onto a sentence it did not follow from. "El parque está cerca de la escuela. Por lo tanto, los niños juegan fútbol." (The park is near the school. Therefore, the kids play soccer.) Therefore promises that the second idea is caused by the first. Being near the school does not cause soccer. Andrés meant "Por lo tanto, muchos niños llegan caminando" (Therefore, many kids arrive on foot), and once he wrote that, the connector made sense.

Addition connectors stack evidence. *Además* (besides, moreover) opens a sentence and adds a new reason: "El campo no tiene luces. Además, la cerca está rota." (The field has no lights. Moreover, the fence is broken.) *También* (also) sits inside the sentence next to the verb: "La cerca también está rota." *Asimismo* (likewise) is the formal version you will see in newspapers. All three add; none of them contrast or conclude.

Conclusion connectors close a chain of reasoning. *Por lo tanto* and *por eso* (that is why) both mean the previous ideas lead here; por lo tanto is more formal. *En conclusión* and *en resumen* (in summary) open a final paragraph. "El campo no tiene luces y la cerca está rota. Por lo tanto, la liga necesita apoyo de la ciudad." (The field has no lights and the fence is broken. Therefore, the league needs support from the city.) The conclusion is earned because two reasons came before it.

Two habits make connectors work. First, punctuation: sin embargo, además, por lo tanto and en cambio at the start of a sentence take a comma after them. Second, variety with restraint. A paragraph with a connector on every sentence reads like a checklist. Use one where the logic turns or lands, and let plain sentences carry the rest. Andrés's final draft has five connectors in four paragraphs, and every one of them points the right way.

words.d: besides, moreover — adds a new reason at the start of a sentence: Además, la cerca está rota
therefore — draws a conclusion from what came before; use only when the earlier ideas cause the new one
that is why, so — the everyday cousin of por lo tanto: Llovió; por eso no jugamos
in summary — opens a closing paragraph that gathers the main points

look.title: Fix the Chain
look.text: Each sentence has a connector; two are wrong. La panadería abre a las cinco. Además, los vecinos compran café temprano. Vende conchas y bolillos. Por lo tanto, también vende pan de muerto en octubre. Mi abuela trabaja doce horas al día. Por lo tanto, está muy cansada por la noche. Sin embargo, nunca se queja. En resumen, la panadería es más que una tienda.
look.prompt: Find the two connectors that promise a relationship the sentences do not have, and replace each with a better one or with nothing.

check.q: El campo no tiene luces. ___, la cerca está rota.
check.why: The second sentence adds a second problem, so it needs the addition connector además.

check.q: Which sentence uses por lo tanto correctly?
choices: Hace calor. Por lo tanto, el parque es grande.
Mi abuela es de Guanajuato. Por lo tanto, la panadería vende café.
Llovió toda la tarde. Por lo tanto, cancelaron el partido.
El pan es barato. Por lo tanto, la tienda está cerca.
check.why: Por lo tanto requires cause and result; rain causing the game to be canceled is the only real chain.

check.q: What does "En resumen, la panadería es más que una tienda" signal to the reader?
choices: A new reason is being added.
The writer is about to give an example.
The writer is gathering the main points to close.
check.why: En resumen means in summary and opens a closing statement that pulls the essay together.

lessons.title: The Error Checklist
lessons.mainIdea: Most essay errors fall into five families, and checking for one family at a time catches more than reading for everything at once.
reading: When Marisol and Andrés listed every circle on their two essays, the mistakes sorted into five piles. Agreement: a noun and its article or adjective did not match. Ser and estar: the wrong verb for a description. Verb endings: the -o ending on a subject that was not yo, or the preterite and imperfect swapped. Accents: a missing mark that changed the word. English word order: an adjective in front of its noun, or a missing personal a. Five families cover most of what an editor will ever find.

*La concordancia* (agreement) errors come from writing fast. "Los panaderías" should be las panaderías; "una problema" should be un problema, because problema is masculine despite its -a. Adjectives follow the noun and take its gender and number: "las conchas frescas," not "las frescas conchas" and not "las conchas fresco." Ser and estar errors come from meaning: "La panadería está en la calle 26" (location, estar), "La panadería es pequeña" (a lasting trait, ser), "El pan está caliente" (a state right now, estar).

Accent errors are silent on the page but loud in meaning. "Hablo" is I speak; "habló" is he or she spoke. "Esta" is this; "está" is he or she is. "Si" is if; "sí" is yes. "Mi" is my; "mí" is me. A reader who meets "mi abuela hablo con el cliente" has to stop and rebuild the sentence. The fix is mechanical: every preterite yo and él form of a regular verb carries an accent, and every question word (qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo) does too.

The last family is English sneaking in. Spanish puts the personal *a* before a person who is the object of the verb: "Conocí a mi amigo," "Vi a mi abuela." It uses tener, not ser, for age: "Tengo diecisiete años." It says "me gusta el pan" with the thing liked as the subject, so the plural is "me gustan las conchas." Reading your own draft aloud is the best test for this family, because a sentence that follows English order will sound like translation.

words.d: agreement — article, noun and adjective share gender and number: las conchas frescas
the problem — masculine despite ending in -a, like el sistema, el tema, el mapa
he or she spoke — the accent separates it from hablo (I speak); regular preterite yo and él forms carry accents
the personal a — placed before a person who receives the action: Vi a mi abuela (I saw my grandmother)
the error, mistake — corregir un error is to correct a mistake; los errores comunes are common errors

look.title: Five Circles
look.text: Andrés's draft, with five errors, one from each family. La liga es en el parque Piotrowski. Tenemos cien niños y veinte entrenadoras muy buenos. El año pasado yo conocí mi mejor amigo allí. Mi padre hablo con la ciudad sobre las luces. Es un grande problema para nosotros.
look.prompt: Find the five errors, name the family each belongs to, and rewrite the paragraph. Which error did you spot last, and why?

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
choices: La panadería está en la calle 26 y es pequeña.
La panadería es en la calle 26 y está pequeña.
La panadería está en la calle 26 y está pequeña.
La panadería es en la calle 26 y es pequeña.
check.why: Location takes estar and a lasting trait like size takes ser, so está en la calle and es pequeña.

check.q: What changes when "Mi abuela hablo con el cliente" becomes "Mi abuela habló con el cliente"?
choices: The verb changes from I speak to she spoke, matching the subject.
The sentence changes from past to present.
The subject changes from my grandmother to me.
check.why: Hablo is the present yo form; the accent makes habló the preterite él or ella form that mi abuela requires.

check.q: Which sentence has an agreement error?
check.why: Entrenadores is masculine plural, so the adjective must be buenos; buenas does not agree.

lessons.title: Reading a Longer Passage
lessons.mainIdea: In a real passage, the verb forms and connectors do work you can trace; reading for them is how you learn to write them.
reading: Before their final drafts, the teacher asks the class to read a passage the way an editor would. Here is the one she gave them, an original piece about a bakery like Marisol's. "Cuando mi abuela llegó a Chicago, no conocía a nadie. Trabajaba de noche en una fábrica y, de día, hacía pan en la cocina de su apartamento. Un vecino le dijo que vendiera las conchas en la iglesia los domingos. Ella dudaba que la gente las comprara. Sin embargo, el primer domingo vendió todo en una hora."

Trace the past tenses. Llegó, dijo and vendió are completed events, each one a step in the story. No conocía, trabajaba and hacía are the background: what her life was like before the story turned. Vendiera and comprara are imperfect subjunctives, one after the recommendation dijo que, one after the doubt dudaba que. And sin embargo marks the turn: she doubted, however she sold out. Five kinds of form in five sentences, every one chosen for a reason.

The passage continues: "Hoy la panadería tiene tres empleados y ha ganado un premio del barrio. Mi abuela ya no amasa el pan; en cambio, enseña a los jóvenes a hacerlo. Quiere que yo aprenda antes de que ella se jubile. Si yo tuviera su paciencia, sería una panadera excelente. Por lo tanto, este verano trabajaré con ella todos los sábados." Tiene and ha ganado bring the story to now. Aprenda and se jubile are present subjunctives after quiere que and antes de que. Tuviera and sería are the if-sentence. Trabajaré is a plan.

Reading this way changes how you write. Once you have traced why an author picked comprara instead of compró, you start asking the same question of your own sentences. The class marks passages with a simple code: P for preterite, I for imperfect, S for subjunctive, C for a connector. After three passages the marks come fast, and the students find they are catching their own errors before the red pen ever comes out.

words.d: the passage — a section of a longer text chosen for reading closely
to retire — a reflexive verb: antes de que ella se jubile (before she retires)
to win a prize — ha ganado un premio is the present perfect: has won a prize
to knead — amasar el pan; the imperfect amasaba describes the daily work in the past

look.title: Mark the Passage
look.text: Mark each verb P, I or S and each connector C. Mi tío aprendió a arreglar hornos cuando tenía quince años. Nadie le enseñó; miraba a los mecánicos del barrio y hacía preguntas. Hoy la gente lo llama cuando algo se rompe. Además, enseña a su hija para que ella sepa hacerlo. Ojalá que yo tuviera esa paciencia. Sin embargo, prefiero hacer pan.
look.prompt: Which sentence has both a connector and a subjunctive? Explain what para que does to the verb after it.

check.q: In "Un vecino le dijo que vendiera las conchas," why is vendiera in the imperfect subjunctive?
choices: Because vender is irregular in the past.
Because the sentence is a question.
Because sin embargo comes before it.
Because dijo que is a past recommendation with a new subject.
check.why: Decir que used as a recommendation triggers the subjunctive, and the past trigger dijo calls for the past form vendiera.

check.q: What does "Ella dudaba que la gente las comprara" mean?
choices: She doubted that people would buy them.
She knew that people bought them.
She hoped that people would buy them.
She said that people were buying them.
check.why: Dudaba que expresses doubt in the past and takes the imperfect subjunctive comprara: she doubted that people would buy them.

check.q: In the passage, which verb marks the turn after sin embargo?
check.why: Sin embargo introduces the completed event that reverses her doubt: vendió todo en una hora.

lessons.title: A Routine for Self-Correction
lessons.mainIdea: Editing your own writing works when it is a fixed routine: one pass per error family, read aloud, then check the connectors last.
reading: The teacher's last lesson before the final draft is not grammar; it is procedure. Nobody catches everything in one reading, so the routine is several short readings, each hunting one thing. Pass one: circle every verb and write its subject above it. Any verb ending in -o with a subject other than yo is a suspect. Pass two: mark every past verb P or I and ask the finished-or-background question. Pass three: find every que and look to its left for a trigger. If there is one, the verb to the right must be subjunctive, present or past to match.

Pass four is agreement and accents, and it goes fastest backward. Reading the essay from the last sentence to the first breaks the flow of meaning, so your eye stops on each word instead of gliding. Check each article against its noun, each adjective against both, and each preterite yo and él form for its accent. Marisol found her "una problema" this way; forward, she had read past it three times.

Pass five is reading aloud, and it is the pass heritage speakers skip and should not. Your ear has heard correct Spanish for years, and it will flag "no creo que viene" or "me gusta las conchas" before your grammar knowledge does. Read at a normal speaking pace and stop wherever you stumble; the stumble is usually a real error. Pass six, the last, is connectors: cover each one, read the two ideas, and ask whether the relationship it promises is really there.

The whole routine takes about fifteen minutes for a one-page essay. Andrés timed it. On his final draft he found four errors himself and his teacher found one more, down from twelve on the draft Marisol edited. "Ya no necesito que alguien me corrija cada línea" (I no longer need someone to correct every line for me), he wrote in his reflection, and then he checked corrija, built from corrijo, and let it stand.

words.d: to correct — an e→i stem-changer with a spelling change: corrijo, corriges; subjunctive corrija
the revision, the editing pass — hacer una revisión is to do a review of a draft
aloud, out loud — leer en voz alta (to read aloud) catches errors your eye slides past
the subject — the person or thing doing the verb; writing it above each verb reveals wrong endings

look.title: Errors Found per Pass
look.cite: Example counts from one student's edit of a one-page draft, as described in this lesson
look.prompt: Which pass found the most errors, and why might reading backward explain that? What does the reading-aloud pass find that the others miss?

check.q: Why does the routine suggest reading the essay backward for agreement and accents?
choices: Because Spanish is read right to left.
Because the last paragraph has the most errors.
Because breaking the flow of meaning makes the eye stop on each word.
Because the verbs are all at the end.
check.why: Reading backward removes the story, so you check each word instead of gliding over it.

check.q: Ya no necesito que alguien me ___ (corregir) cada línea.
check.why: Necesitar que with a new subject triggers the present subjunctive; corregir builds corrija from the yo form corrijo.

check.q: In pass three, what do you look for to the left of every que?
choices: A trigger such as quiero, dudo or es importante.
check.why: A trigger before que is what sends the following verb into the subjunctive, so that is what the pass hunts for.

review.why: Ver has the irregular participle visto, and the yo helper is he: he visto, I have seen.

review.q: Mientras mi abuela ___ (amasar) el pan, sonó el teléfono.
review.why: Mientras marks an action in progress that another event interrupts, so it takes the imperfect amasaba.
Venir uses the shortened stem vendr- in the future, and the ellos ending is -án: vendrán.
Es necesario que is an impersonal trigger with a new subject, and ser has the irregular subjunctive seas.
An imagined if-sentence uses the imperfect subjunctive after si: pudiera, built from pudieron.

review.q: El campo no tiene luces. ___, la cerca está rota.
review.why: A second problem is being added, so the addition connector además fits; nothing is contrasted or concluded.

review.q: Which sentence has an error in the personal a?
choices: Vi a mi abuela en la panadería.
Conocí a mi mejor amigo allí.
Llamé a mi tío por teléfono.
Escuché mi prima en el concierto.
review.why: Mi prima is a person receiving the action, so the sentence needs the personal a: Escuché a mi prima.

review.q: What does "Aunque llueve, jugamos" say that "Aunque llueva, jugaremos" does not?
choices: That the rain is a fact right now, not a possibility.
That the speaker doubts it will rain.
That the speaker wishes it would rain.
review.why: The indicative llueve after aunque concedes a known fact, even though it is raining; the subjunctive llueva presents rain as only possible.
